reframing_when: The question asks how to continue or improve an existing commitment without considering whether abandoning it is the better move — past investment is anchoring the question.
The question frames stopping as 'failure' or 'waste' rather than as a rational reallocation of future resources — the negative framing of quitting is distorting the inquiry.

The question asks 'how do we make this work?' for a project with accumulating evidence of failure, instead of asking 'if we were starting fresh today with no prior investment, would we still choose this path?'
The question escalates commitment to a chosen course ('how do we go deeper?') when the escalation itself is the problem — knee-deep-in-the-big-muddy dynamics.
reframing_move: Apply the fresh-start test: ask 'if we had no history with this and were deciding today from scratch, would we start this?' — marginal analysis strips away the emotional weight of past investment and forces the question to be about future value only.
curation_note: Sunk cost fallacy is a reframing tool because it converts backward-looking questions (how do we justify what we've spent) into forward-looking ones (what is the best use of our next dollar/hour). Distinct from inversion — sunk cost specifically targets the temporal distortion where past investment corrupts present decision framing.

reframing_when.note: All four activations grounded: anchoring on past investment (core definition), negative framing of quitting (sinking ship analogy), fresh-start test (marginal analysis framework), escalating commitment (knee-deep-in-the-big-muddy).

frame_patterns_challenged.note: Commitment escalation is the primary target. Temporal fixation: the question is locked into the past rather than evaluating future value.
